Central Cascades.author: Aaron Hartz
Central Cascades.bottom_line:
The Central Oregon Avalanche Center has concluded operations for the 2025/26 season. 

There is still a lot of riding to be had in the mountains. The corn cycle is on, and the upper elevations still have good snow coverage. There is a lot of terrain to explore in the central Oregon mountains.

Keep in mind we can still have conditions that lead to avalanches. Wet loose avalanches are a common theme during these warmer months. On the warm sunny days, use timing to your advantage to get the good riding but keep an eye on how deep the snow is becoming wet and slushy. If you start sinking into wet slushy snow, it is a good idea to move to more shaded slopes or lower angle terrain. Wet loose avalanches can increase in size during those periods of warm nights without a surface refreeze. 

It is not uncommon to get snow storms in the mountains during the spring and summer months. When this happens, we can see a return of winter-type avalanche problems. When the snow falls, keep wind slab avalanches on your radar. With enough new snow, storm slabs can also make a comeback. Following spring snow storms when the temperature warms up we often get a cycle of wet snow problems with wet slabs and wet loose avalanches that can be larger than normal. 

Other hazards that are associated with spring riding include rockfall and lingering cornices that can break off. Remember to look above you and recognize overhead hazards. 

If you see avalanches or signs of unstable snow, or just good riding conditions, please take a few minutes to post an observation on the COAC website.

Check our website in the fall as the days become shorter and the nights get colder. We will have updates about fundraisers, events, educational opportunities, and more.

On behalf of all of us at COAC, we would like to thank the members, supporters, local businesses, and organizations that keep us going. We are entirely funded by this community of great people.  Without you, we would not be here. It has been a pleasure serving the central Oregon backcountry community this season. 

We will be back in action starting on December 1st when we begin issuing daily forecasts for the 2026/27 season!

Newberry.author: Gabriel Coler
Newberry.bottom_line:
Regular avalanche forecasts have come to an end for the Newberry National Monument.  It sure wasn't the greatest winter that I've had up in the monument, but I did find good riding more often than I expected throughout the winter.  The snowpack up at Paulina is pretty darn thin and the road has naturally melted out to past the lodge.  Conditions feel at least a month ahead of where they usually are (late March feels like late April of last year).  Avalanches can still occur on steep slopes, and there is even some snow in the forecast for this first week of April.

Most of our spring-time avalanche activity is related to warm temperatures and sunshine, which melt the snow.  This is the same melting that we rely on for soft riding conditions, but when there is too much free water in the snowpack, or very warm temperatures are heating more recently fallen snow, then we start to see Wet avalanches.  Most of these are predictable because we can feel how slushy the surface snow is as we travel (or in the case of warming on newer snow, we can see pinwheels).  It is worth remembering that even small Wet avalanches can be powerful enough to knock a rider off their feet, which can be problematic in terrain where you'd rather not fall.

Often we experience spring snow storms.  If you find yourself riding in conditions that feel more wintry than spring-like, consider those avalanche problems that we associate with winter riding.  Unlike in the Cascades, these spring storms are less likely to drop enough snow at Paulina to produce big avalanche cycles, but it's not out of the question.

We will begin operations for the 2026/27 winter season on December 1.  Please check back for observations during the spring, or during the fall if we are lucky enough for some good early season riding!  The avalanche center also hosts lots of cool events during the pre-season:  Know-Before-You-Go avalanche seminars, the Bend Snow and Avalanche Workshop, "Beacon and Eggs" avalanche rescue class, movies, etc.  Check out our web-site for details.

Thanks to our forecast team and volunteer board of directors.  Thank you to OSSA, the Dodgers, and the crew at Octane for all the support.  Psyched to see everyone next winter, and hoping it'll be better than this last one!
